title: HEPA vs MERV Filters: Which Is Better for HVAC?
h1: Which Is Better for Your HVAC System: HEPA or MERV Filters?
description: HEPA filters catch more but usually choke a home HVAC system. A good MERV filter is the better fit for most homes. Here is how to choose the right one.
quick_answer: For most home HVAC systems, a quality MERV filter is the better choice. HEPA filters trap finer particles, but they're so dense that a standard residential blower can't push enough air through them. If you want HEPA-level filtration, use a portable HEPA purifier or a whole-home bypass unit built for it.
body:
HEPA sounds like the gold standard, and for capturing fine particles it is. But a filter only helps if air can actually get through it. In a typical home system, the right MERV filter catches most of what matters without starving the blower of air.

What is the difference between HEPA and MERV?

MERV stands for Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value. It's a rating scale from 1 to 16 that shows how well a filter captures particles of different sizes. Higher numbers catch smaller particles. Most home filters fall between MERV 6 and MERV 13.

HEPA stands for High Efficiency Particulate Air. It's not a point on the MERV scale. It's a separate, stricter standard for filters that capture nearly all very fine particles. HEPA filters are used in hospitals, labs and many portable air purifiers.

Why don't most homes use HEPA filters in the HVAC system?

HEPA media is very dense. Home furnaces and air handlers are designed to move a certain amount of air against a certain amount of resistance. A HEPA filter in a standard filter slot adds far more resistance than the blower was built for.

That causes real problems:

  • Less air reaches your rooms, so comfort drops
  • The AC coil can freeze from low airflow
  • The furnace can overheat and shut down on its safety limit
  • The blower motor works harder and may wear out sooner
  • Air leaks around the filter edges instead of through it

Most HEPA filters also don't come in the common 1-inch sizes that fit residential grilles, which is a hint that they weren't meant for that spot.

Which MERV rating should I use?

Here's a practical guide for homes:

MERV ratingWhat it catchesGood fit for
MERV 1 to 4Large dust and lintProtecting equipment only
MERV 5 to 8Dust, pollen, mold spores, pet hairMost homes as a baseline
MERV 9 to 12Finer dust, some pet danderHomes with pets or mild allergies
MERV 13Fine particles, including much of the smoke-size rangeAllergies, asthma and wildfire season, if the system can handle it

MERV 13 is often recommended for wildfire smoke, and a lot of San Diego and Orange County homeowners ask about it during fire season. The catch is airflow. A 1-inch MERV 13 filter can be too restrictive for some systems, especially older ones with small returns. A thicker 4- or 5-inch media filter at the same rating has more surface area and much less resistance.

How do I get HEPA-level filtration at home?

If you or someone in your home needs the cleanest possible air, you have options that don't put the system at risk:

  1. Portable HEPA purifiers. Good for bedrooms and main living areas. Size the unit to the room.
  2. Whole-home bypass HEPA units. These pull part of the air from the duct system, filter it through HEPA media with their own fan, then send it back. Your main blower isn't fighting the HEPA filter.
  3. A media filter upgrade. Pairing a deep MERV 13 cabinet with a good portable purifier covers most needs.

How do I know if my filter is too restrictive?

Watch for weak airflow from the vents, a whistling return grille, a filter bowing inward, or an AC that ices up. A technician can measure the static pressure across the filter to see how much it's restricting the system. That's the most reliable way to know whether a higher MERV filter is safe for your equipment.

Does a better filter fix everything?

A filter only cleans air that passes through it, and only while the system runs. If the fan sits idle most of the day, so does your filter. Leaky return ducts can pull dusty attic air in after the filter. Odors and gases need carbon or ventilation, not particle filtration. Mold and humidity problems need moisture control.

Our indoor air quality team can check your system's airflow and recommend the right filter, media cabinet or purifier for your home.
faqs: Is MERV 13 too high for my home system?

It depends on the system. Many systems handle a MERV 13 media filter that's 4 or 5 inches thick, but a 1-inch MERV 13 can restrict airflow in some homes. A technician can measure static pressure to tell you for sure.

No. HEPA filters capture particles, not gases or odors. For smells, look for a purifier with a substantial activated carbon filter, and deal with the source, such as moisture, pets or a dirty drain pan.
What MERV rating is best for wildfire smoke?

MERV 13 is commonly recommended for smoke, as long as your system can handle the airflow. During heavy smoke, keep windows closed, run the fan to keep air moving through the filter and use a portable HEPA purifier in bedrooms.
Is a washable filter better than a disposable one?

Usually not. Most washable filters are low on the MERV scale and catch mainly large dust. They also need to dry completely before going back in, or they can grow mold. A good disposable or media filter usually filters better.
